page.h1: HTS Chapter 10: Cereals — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Chapter 10 Export Markets: Tariffs on U.S. Grain by Country
seo.shortDescription: The tariff each top buyer charges on U.S. corn, wheat, rice and sorghum, with the trade agreement and plant-health regulator for each.

intro: Almost every large buyer takes U.S. grain duty-free or close to it. Mexico and Canada charge nothing under USMCA, South Korea and Colombia charge nothing on corn and wheat under their agreements, Japan admits feed corn and sorghum free, and the EU sets its grain duty by a formula that is often zero. Japan's wheat and rice, and Korea's rice, move only through state-run quotas. What decides access is more often a plant-health certificate or a biotech approval than a tariff.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

markets.name: Japan
markets.rule: Japan's customs tariff; U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement; state trading for wheat, barley and rice

1001.rate: Free in the state-run quota, plus a government mark-up
1001.basis: Japan's state-trading wheat system: no duty inside the quota, with a government mark-up paid by the miller (about 17 yen/kg in the TPP-era baseline, cut by 45% over nine years under the CPTPP-equivalent terms). The U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement also gives U.S. wheat a country-specific quota. Confirm the current mark-up with USDA FAS.

1002.rate: Free (U.S.–Japan agreement; 4.2% normal rate removed in 2019)
1002.basis: USDA FAS, USJTA Treatment for Coarse Grains (JA2020-0045): rye went from a 4.2% normal rate to free in 2019.

1003.rate: Free in the state-run quota, plus a government mark-up
1003.basis: USDA FAS, USJTA Treatment for Coarse Grains (JA2020-0045): government-imported barley is free subject to a WTO mark-up that falls to a maximum of 4.4 yen/kg in 2026.

1004.rate: Not individually verified — see the market's tariff schedule
1004.basis: Japan Customs Tariff 2026; a small group (under 1% of the chapter), check the national line

1005.basis: USDA FAS, USJTA Treatment for Coarse Grains (JA2020-0045): feed corn stays at 0%, and the 3.0% normal rate on other corn went to free in 2019.

1006.rate: Quota only: 341 yen/kg above the minimum-access quota
1006.basis: Japan Customs Tariff 2026: rice was excluded from tariff elimination. Imports inside the WTO minimum-access quota (682,200 tonnes of milled rice) pay a government mark-up; above it the duty is 341 yen/kg. U.S. rice is bought inside the quota.

1007.basis: USDA FAS, USJTA Treatment for Coarse Grains (JA2020-0045): grain sorghum went from a 3.0% normal rate to free in 2019.

1008.rate: Buckwheat free since 2023; other lines not verified
1008.basis: USDA FAS, USJTA Treatment for Coarse Grains (JA2020-0045): buckwheat went from a 9.0% normal rate to free in 2023. Millet, canary seed and other cereals in this heading are not individually verified.

profile.headline: Japan buys corn and sorghum duty-free for feed, but wheat and rice are state-managed: wheat enters through a government-run quota with a mark-up, and rice through a small minimum-access quota.
profile.tariffNow: Feed corn and sorghum free; wheat and rice through quotas

assumptions: Rates come from each market's trade-agreement schedule (USMCA, KORUS, U.S.–Colombia TPA) or its own customs tariff, with USDA Foreign Agricultural Service reports used for Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.

One representative subheading stands in for each four-digit group (corn 1005.90, wheat 1001.99, rice 1006.30). Smaller groups (rye, barley, oats and the grains in 1008 — together under 1% of the chapter) carry a market-wide rate where it is known and are marked 'not individually verified' where it is not.

Japan's wheat and barley move through a state-trading system: the tariff is zero in the quota, and the government adds a mark-up that is the real cost. That mark-up, and the Philippines, Taiwan and EU grain rates, are shown as described in the cited source and should be confirmed on the national tariff line.

The EU sets its import duty on maize, sorghum and rye by a formula tied to world prices (Regulation (EU) No 642/2010), so it changes with the market and is sometimes zero. Check the Commission's current notice.
National 8–10-digit tariff lines can set a different rate than the six-digit subheading shown here — check the market's own schedule before relying on this page for a transaction.
